mappings.note: Separates pilgrimage, undertaken for spiritual reasons, from tourism for leisure. Religious practice, so LO-150.
Seeing the landscape as punyakshetra is credited with protecting and preserving nature. The conservation payoff is what the item tests, so LO-146.
Community protection of groves read as reverence and interdependence with nature. Conservation sensitivity, the outcome's own language.
Local claims that epic heroes passed through a locality let communities make pan-Indian narratives their own. A religious and cultural tradition, so LO-150.

Distinguishes a relic stupa enshrining bodily remains from a commemorative one - a difference in the purpose and construction of a religious monument, which LO-149 covers. The frame names tombs, and a relic stupa is exactly that.
Matches amrita manthana, tirthankara, jyotirlinga and takht to their traditions. Religious concepts across faiths.
A Western Ghats grove protected for a forest deity preserving rare species. Biodiversity conservation through sacred protection, so LO-146.

The keyed wrong action is unregulated industrial discharge near a sacred site, against cleaning polluted rivers and sustainable practice. That is pollution and the measures against it, so LO-145 rather than the broader conservation outcome.
Matches traditions to their sacred concepts and rejects Tirthankaras as Sikh. Religious traditions throughout.
Tirthas sitting on rivers and mountains because such landscapes are themselves held sacred. The reasoning is about a religious perception, so LO-150.
Statements on the Nadistuti hymn, the spread of sacred groves and Bhudevi. Religious traditions, keyed on the Bhudevi statement.
Links the amrita manthana legend to the Kumbh Mela. Religious mythology under LO-150.
Shakti Pithas as the places where parts of Sati fell. Religious tradition of the Divine Feminine.

Taranaki Maunga as the Maori ancestral mountain. A sacred-geography belief from another culture, so LO-150; the item on granting such a mountain legal rights was given LO-146 because it concerns protection.
Matching across Char Dham, jyotirlingas, Shakti Pithas and Sikh takhts. Religious networks of several traditions.
The set pairs Bhudevi and the sangam as religious concepts (LO-150) with sacred groves and the Peepul as protected natural features (LO-146). Both lanes appear in the same item.
Matching across Buddhist sites, Jain tirthas, Guru Nanak's travels and Sabarimala. Religious traditions and their sacred places.
Defines pilgrimage as a journey to a place of spiritual value. The chapter's central religious practice.
Contrasts the scale of the Kumbh with a local temple festival. A comparison of religious gatherings, so LO-150.
Names Sati as the goddess of the Shakti Pitha legend. Religious mythology under LO-150.
A harmonious relationship with sacred geography resolved into shared values and respect for the environment. The answer is an environmental ethic, so LO-146 rather than the religion outcome.
Analyses sacredness across shrines, rivers, mountains, journeys, routes and the land itself. The chapter's core religious idea in its widest form.
Part (i) asks why Prayagraj is sacred (LO-150), while parts (ii) and (iii) turn on preventing pollution of the Ganga and Yamuna during a mass gathering and what organisers should do (LO-145).
A Jyotirlinga circuit distinguished from tourism, with cultural encounter and inner discipline. Religious practice throughout, so LO-150.
Part (i) is about the ecological roles of an oran (LO-146), while the clearing and the industrial waste dumped into its water body are pollution and degradation (LO-145). Both are examined.
Compares Indian sacred geography with Maori and Native American traditions. A comparison of religious worldviews, so LO-150.
Evaluates legal personhood for rivers and mountains as a conservation strategy. The question is explicitly about protecting nature, so LO-146.
The epics weaving local landscapes into a pan-Indian sacred narrative. Religious and cultural tradition, so LO-150.

Sets the inner discipline of pilgrimage against the commercialisation of mass tourism. The tension examined is spiritual rather than ecological, so LO-150 rather than LO-146, though crowding is mentioned in passing.
Sacred geography as the backbone of cultural identity through pilgrimage networks, rivers and local traditions. Religious idea shaping culture, so LO-150.
The full analysis of Suzuki's argument that seeing nature as kin rather than resource changes how we act. Conservation sensitivity, like the short-answer version of the same passage.

The Dongria Khond case turns on a mountain held to be a deity's abode (LO-150) and on a mining project that would destroy both the hill and their sustenance (LO-146). Part (iii) asks the learner to weigh cultural and environmental claims together.
The significance of the takhts as Sikh seats of authority and pilgrimage. Religious institution under LO-150.
Tirtha as a symbolic crossing to a higher state. The chapter's central religious concept.
Pilgrimage across the subcontinent binding India into one cultural unit. A consequence of religious practice, so LO-150.
Why places tied to the Tirthankaras are sacred in Jainism. Doctrine and sacred site together, so LO-150.
Explains Bhudevi as the earth personified as a goddess. A religious conception of the planet; the items that turn it into action on nature carry LO-146.
Why the Dongria Khond hold Niyam Dongar sacred - the abode of Niyam Raja who sustains them. Religious belief, so LO-150; the mining case study adds LO-146 because protection is at stake there.
The Char Dham network sanctifying the whole expanse of the country. A pilgrimage system, so LO-150.
The Shakti Pitha story turning the landmass into the goddess's body. Religious symbolism under LO-150.
Pilgrimage fostering understanding across languages and customs. Cultural effect of a religious practice, so LO-150.
Rivers revered as goddesses, with the Nadistuti sukta as evidence of how old the reverence is. Religious tradition; not LO-146, because no conservation measure is asked.
The churning legend and the four places where drops of amrita fell. Religious mythology behind a pilgrimage.

Trade routes running past Buddhist, Jain and Hindu sites, and merchants endowing them, used to argue for tolerance and exchange. Economic and cultural history, so the history goal rather than the religion outcome.
